story.card_text: Two women, Joyce Kalina and Paula Kelley, opened Club Mount Auburn 47 on January 6, 1958, at 47 Mount Auburn Street, as a coffeehouse and jazz club. The Steve Kuhn Trio played opening night. Then the folk singers showed up. Joan Baez, a seventeen-year-old Boston University student, gave her first professional performance at the club, and she and Eric von Schmidt were among the first folk singers who turned it from jazz to folk. Bill Monroe recruited three of his Blue Grass Boys there. In the fall of 1963 the club moved to this lane, and the post office designated the new address 47 Palmer Street so it could keep its name. Now the legend: Bob Dylan played Club 47. Sort of. The folklorist who supplied the Globe's history says he never had featured billing; he got up as a guest of Eric von Schmidt and of Baez. The club closed on April 28, 1968, the room became a campaign office for Eugene McCarthy, and music came back in 1969 under the name Passim. It has been a nonprofit, Club Passim, since 1995.

story.narration_script: You're in Palmer Street, Harvard Square. In January of nineteen fifty-eight, two women opened a coffeehouse and jazz club at forty-seven Mount Auburn Street and named it after the address: Club forty-seven. Then the folk singers arrived. Joan Baez, a seventeen-year-old Boston University student, played her first professional show there. Bill Monroe hired three of his Blue Grass Boys out of that room. In nineteen sixty-three the club moved here, and the post office gave the new place the number forty-seven again, so the name still worked. Now, the legend. People say Bob Dylan played Club forty-seven. He did, sort of. According to the Globe's history, he never got his name on the bill. He got up as a guest of other singers, including Baez. The club closed in April of nineteen sixty-eight. Music came back the next year, and it's been Club Passim ever since.

seo.landing_copy: Boston has always been loud in specific rooms. This walk goes to them. It starts at a stone meeting house in the South End that spent two and a half years as the Boston Tea Party, the room where the Velvet Underground felt at home and Led Zeppelin made their debut in town. It follows Storyville, George Wein's jazz club, from a hotel on Huntington Avenue to Kenmore Square and back, and stops over the cellar on Boylston Street where two clubs shared one staircase and a lot of famous people played before they were famous. In Kenmore you stand where the Rat was, and on Lansdowne Street you find out what the same address has been through since it was a taxi garage behind the Green Monster. Then it turns to the halls: the movie house Berklee bought, the concert hall a Harvard physicist helped design, a department-store family's gift to the Conservatory, and the opera house that left nothing but a street name. It ends on Mass Ave at the one club on the old Jazz Corner of Boston that's still open. Every stop has a riddle that gets you there and an answer you read off the building, and every story comes with its sources, including the ones that correct what you've heard. The walk is about two and three-quarter hours, flat and step-free, and there's a one-hour short cut through the Symphony and Mass Ave stops. Two detours go out to Aerosmith's old Allston apartment and Club Passim in Harvard Square. Any two stops are free.

story.card_text: On December 12, 1968, Lou Reed called this old church the Velvet Underground's 'favorite place to play in the whole country.' From January 20, 1967, the meeting house on this corner was the Boston Tea Party, with Ray Riepen running it and the Boston band the Lost on the first bill. It had been showing underground films; the weekend dance concerts were supposed to pay for them. Within two years Led Zeppelin had made their Tea Party debut and B.B. King had played the room. Now look up at the star in the window. That star is why you'll read, on Wikipedia among other places, that this was built as a synagogue. The marker by the door says it went up in 1872 as a Unitarian meeting house named for Theodore Parker, and that the star was about bringing the world's religions together. Second story you'll hear: WBCN, the station that made Boston an album-rock town, started in the Tea Party's back room. Riepen founded the station too, but its own people put the first studio upstairs at 171 Newbury Street and call the back-room version a myth. The club moved to Lansdowne Street in July 1969. You'll see that block later.

story.look_now: The star in the window, then the marker by the door. Same building, two different stories about it.
story.narration_script: Look up at the window on the front of this old church. In December of nineteen sixty-eight, Lou Reed called this place the Velvet Underground's favorite place to play in the whole country. It opened as a rock club called the Boston Tea Party on January twentieth, nineteen sixty-seven. Within two years Led Zeppelin had played their first Tea Party shows here, and B B King had worked the room. Now, that star in the window. It's the reason people say this was built as a synagogue. The marker by the door says no: it went up in eighteen seventy-two as a Unitarian meeting house, named for the abolitionist minister Theodore Parker, and the star was about bringing the world's religions together. One more story people tell is that the rock station W B C N started in the club's back room. The man who ran the club did found the station. But the station's own people say its first studio was upstairs on Newbury Street, and they call the back-room story a myth. In July of nineteen sixty-nine the club moved to Lansdowne Street, by Fenway Park. You'll get there later.

story.card_text: Charlie Parker was booked to play this hotel on March 12, 1955. He died in New York that night. The room was Storyville, and George Wein had opened it here in October 1950, at twenty-five, naming it after New Orleans' old red-light district. About six weeks in he fell out with the landlord and closed. He reopened in Kenmore Square in February 1951, came back here in September 1953 under new hotel owners, and shut it for good in May 1960. In between, Louis Armstrong, Billie Holiday, Miles Davis, Ella Fitzgerald, Thelonious Monk and Lester Young played Storyville. The founder, Lawrence Berk, went to MIT, studied architectural engineering and worked for Raytheon. On the side he studied music in New York with Joseph Schillinger, a theorist whose students included George Gershwin and Glenn Miller, and became one of only twelve people Schillinger authorized to teach his method. He started with three students. In 1945 he bought a three-story building at 284 Newbury Street and named the school Schillinger House, after his teacher. Berklee calls it the first institution of higher education in the US founded on the study of jazz. By 1947 it was authorized to take students on the GI Bill. story.card_text: The hall the Boston Symphony left in 1900, by one account because it was going to be torn down, is still standing, at the end of this lane. The Boston Music Hall opened here on November 20, 1852, and when Henry Lee Higginson founded the Boston Symphony Orchestra in 1881, this was its home. In 1863 the hall got a giant German organ, built by Walcker of Ludwigsburg. In the summer of 1884 it was pulled out to make room for the orchestra, over protests that went as far as legal action. Then an urban development project put the hall on the schedule to be closed and razed, and the orchestra left for Huntington Avenue in 1900. That's the story Symphony Hall's landmark nomination tells. Here's the correction: nobody tore it down. It went vaudeville in 1900, and in 1916 Thomas Lamb, the architect of the Fenway Theatre at stop 8, rebuilt it as Loew's Orpheum, which its history calls Boston's first authentic movie palace. Sarah Caldwell's opera company used it in the 1970s. Now it's a 2,700-seat rock room, and Don Law took his shows here when the Tea Party closed in 1970.

summary: In 1978 the city took a jazz club on Mass Ave for a highway it never built, so Wally's moved across the street and kept going. This walk reads Boston's music history off the buildings: the church that became the Boston Tea Party, the cellar where Springsteen was the opening act, the hotel that replaced the Rat, the hall a physicist tuned and the opera house that left a street sign. Some of the rooms are gone. Some still sell tickets tonight.
